developer setup

One temporary shell. Nothing to undo.

Download pkgreg-client and run one command. It opens a child shell in this terminal with your package tools already pointed at this cache. Type exit when you are done.

Six commands Explain each one

No sudo, no CA installation, no cache IP, no insecure TLS flag.

while the child shell is open
✓the cache’s CA is fingerprint-verified
✓pip, uv and npm use a localhost bridge
✓Git, files and apt get temporary addresses
✓no system or project files are changed

Your commands, top to bottom.

Pick your platform and run the column. Every address, project and fingerprint is already this instance’s own. Everything below this section is the same steps with the reasons attached.

first, for every platform

Download pkgreg-client

Choose your build5 platforms

Linux

The daemon shares your loopback, so nothing here involves a certificate.

  1. Make it runnable

    chmod +x pkgreg-client

  2. Open the shell

    ./pkgreg-client -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"

    temporary session ready means you are in. exit undoes everything.

  3. Install packages as usual

    python -m pip install six uv pip install six npm install left-pad sudo apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$PKGREG_APT_PROXY" update

  4. Pull images

    docker pull "$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20"

  5. Build images

    pkgreg-client build -t myapp:dev . pkgreg-client compose build

    Your Dockerfile is never modified. Add -print to see what it would build.

  6. Optional — builds you start another way

    pkgreg-client -docker-build-trust

    Once, then apt and apk reach the cache from any build on this machine — a Makefile, an IDE, Compose.

macOS

Docker Desktop runs in a VM that cannot see your loopback, so Docker uses the cache’s own address.

  1. Make it runnable

    chmod +x pkgreg-client

  2. Open the shell

    ./pkgreg-client -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"

  3. Install packages as usual

    python -m pip install six uv pip install six npm install left-pad

  4. Teach Docker the cache, once

    ./pkgreg-client -docker-trust -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"

    No sudo. Restart Docker Desktop afterwards.

  5. Pull images

    docker pull cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20

  6. Build images

    pkgreg-client build -cache-address -t myapp:dev . pkgreg-client compose -cache-address build

    -cache-address mounts the CA into each step that needs it — never written into a layer.

Windows

PowerShell, and Docker Desktop takes registry trust from the Windows certificate store rather than a directory.

  1. Rename it

    Rename-Item pkgreg-client-windows-amd64.exe pkgreg-client.exe

    There is no chmod step.

  2. Open the shell

    .\pkgreg-client.exe -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"

    A normal window is enough; Administrator is not needed for this.

  3. Install packages as usual

    python -m pip install six uv pip install six npm install left-pad

  4. For Docker, an Administrator PowerShell, once

    .\pkgreg-client.exe --persist -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"

    -docker-trust does not work here: a per-registry folder would have to be named <host>:<port>, and a colon cannot appear in a Windows path. Open a new terminal afterwards.

  5. Pull images

    docker pull cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20

  6. Build images

    pkgreg-client build -cache-address -t myapp:dev .

    Working in WSL2? Use the Linux column for everything except this — the daemon is still Docker Desktop’s.

that is the whole setup

Something failed, or you want to know why any of it is shaped this way? Start walks the same steps slowly, Docker covers builders and CI, and Troubleshooting lists the errors by message.

new — one binary, three places to look

Or cache on this machine too.

pkgcache is this client with a cache of its own. A lookup goes to your machine first, then to this server, then to the public registry — so a second npm ci costs nothing, and a morning when this server is down costs you a slower build rather than a stopped one.

Once

Set it up

Verifies this server’s CA against the fingerprint below, sets a disk budget, and writes nothing outside its own directory.

pkgcache setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -limit 25G
Every day

Use it

Starts the cache if it is not running. Nothing is installed and nothing outlives the command.

pkgcache run -- npm ci
Anytime

See what it is doing

Reports all three tiers, and says plainly when this server is unreachable rather than letting builds quietly get slower.

pkgcache status

It never deletes anything on its own. The limit is asked for once and never guessed. When the cache is full it keeps serving and stops storing, says so on stderr, in status and as a desktop notification, and exits 75 — so a pipeline that has quietly stopped caching goes red instead of getting slower. pkgcache prune is the only thing that removes anything.

Falling back is deliberate, not automatic. A refused connection, a timeout or a server error moves to the next place to look. A 404 does not — that is what a cache in offline mode answers, and going around it would defeat an air gap somebody switched on. Nor does a 403, which is a credential problem worth seeing once rather than never. pkgcache setup -no-direct removes the public registry from the chain entirely.

Want only what the shell below does? pkgcache setup -no-cache -server … -ca-sha256 … is exactly that: a verified loopback bridge, no local store, no database. Nothing is written to disk beyond the settings themselves.

the first three steps, in full · about two minutes

Download the client, start the shell, then exit.

Every command on this page is already filled in for this cache and for project global — the addresses and the fingerprint below are this instance’s own, not examples. If your team uses a different project, open Console → Connect and copy the command shown there instead.

This cache is not serving TLS, so the client cannot connect to it yet.

pkgreg-client only accepts an https:// server: it fetches the CA over one unverified request, pins it to the fingerprint, and verifies everything after that. Against an http:// address it stops with server must use https. Nothing you can pass on the command line changes this, and no insecure flag is the answer.

The operator fixes it on the cache host: pkgreg init mints the certificate pair into the data directory, and a server started against that data directory picks it up on restart. pkgreg doctor reports the missing pair as a failure.

  1. 1

    Download pkgreg-client

    One executable, not an installer. Most Intel and AMD machines are amd64; Apple silicon is darwin arm64.

    served by this pkgreg instance

    Client downloads

    checking

    Looking for published client binaries…

    Linux or macOS

    Rename it, make it executable, and check it arrived intact — the expected digest is printed under each download button above.

    mv pkgreg-client-<os>-<arch> pkgreg-client chmod +x pkgreg-client sha256sum pkgreg-client # shasum -a 256 on macOS

    Windows

    Rename it to pkgreg-client.exe, then check the digest. A normal PowerShell window is enough; Administrator is not needed.

    Get-FileHash .\pkgreg-client.exe -Algorithm SHA256
  2. 2

    Check the fingerprint, then start the shell

    This is the SHA-256 of this cache’s public certificate authority. Compare it with the value your operator gave you through a separate trusted channel — a chat message, a wiki page, anything that is not this page. That comparison is what makes the connection safe; the client refuses to continue if it does not match.

    CA SHA-256 · this instance Open Console → Connect to copy the fingerprint
    Linux and macOS
    ./pkgreg-client -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"
    Windows PowerShell
    .\pkgreg-client.exe -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"
    If your project requires an access token, this command fails with 401 until you add one. Create a read token in Console → Connect, save the one-time secret to a file, restrict it with chmod 600 pkgreg.token, and add -token-file ./pkgreg.token to the command above. Connect shows the exact command with the flag already included when the project needs it.
  3. 3

    Work in the new shell, then type exit

    A temporary session ready message means the localhost bridge is running. You are now in a child shell — the same directory, the same files, different package settings. Exiting stops the bridge and returns you to the parent terminal exactly as it was.

    python -m pip install six exit

What the shell actually changed

Only environment variables, only in that child shell. Nothing is written to your home directory, your project, or the operating system — which is why there is no uninstall step. Print them at any time:

env | grep ^PKGREG_ | sort
  • PIP_INDEX_URL, UV_DEFAULT_INDEX, NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY — why pip, uv and npm need no flags
  • PKGREG_GIT_URL, PKGREG_FILES_URL, PKGREG_APT_PROXY — the addresses used by the commands in the next section
  • PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY — the image registry, covered under Docker
  • PKGREG_BRIDGE_URL — the loopback bridge itself, on a port chosen fresh for each session

Because that port is new every time, never paste a bridge address into a file that outlives the session — a Dockerfile, a lockfile, a CI config. Reference the variable, or use the direct cache address described under shared hosts.

inside the pkgreg shell

Use normal package commands.

The client already set the variables these tools read. Use them exactly as you would without a cache.

Python

pip

python -m pip install six
Python

uv

uv pip install six
Node

npm

npm install left-pad
Source

Git

Keep the original host in the path; the mirror is read-only.

git clone "$PKGREG_GIT_URL/github.com/pallets/click.git"
Artifacts

Files

Replace <path> with a file your team has uploaded. Downloads are anonymous; uploading needs a write token.

wget "${PKGREG_FILES_URL}<path>"
System

apt and apk

Here sudo is for changing operating-system packages, not for pkgreg — the client setup itself stays unprivileged.

sudo apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$PKGREG_APT_PROXY" update
Do not add TLS workarounds. No --trusted-host, no --insecure, no CA path, no cache IP. The bridge is plain HTTP on your own loopback interface and the hop to the cache is verified TLS, so every such flag only removes a check that is already passing. If a tool reports a certificate error, the fingerprint or the address is wrong — see Troubleshooting.
Different package, project or ecosystem? Console → Connect generates the same commands from this instance’s live configuration, for whichever project you select. This page is the explanation; Connect is the lookup.

containers

Docker plays by different rules.

Everything above works because the client changed your shell’s environment. Docker does not read your shell: the daemon is a separate, long-running process, and it — not your terminal — resolves image names and runs build steps. So each Docker task needs its address passed in explicitly. Three cases cover all of it.

  1. A

    Pull and run images

    Works from the temporary shell with Docker running on this same Linux machine. The daemon shares your loopback interface, and Docker already treats a 127.0.0.1 registry as a local one, so nothing has to be configured or trusted first.

    docker pull "$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20"

    Every image name is <upstream>/<repo>:<tag>. Choose the upstream with the first path segment — the rest is the image’s normal path on that registry:

    • dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20 — Docker Hub. Official images live under library/ (so alpine is library/alpine).
    • dockerhub/grafana/grafana:11.1.0 — a Hub image that keeps its <org>/<image> namespace.
    • dockerhub/library/postgres:16, dockerhub/library/redis:7, dockerhub/library/node:22-alpine — more official images.
    • ghcr/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim — GitHub Container Registry.
    • quay/prometheus/busybox:latest — Quay.
    • nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.01 — any other registry, named by its host. Nothing has to be configured first: write the registry’s hostname where dockerhub would go and the cache fetches from it.

    Pin by digest for reproducibility. A tag can move; a digest cannot. The cache stores each blob by digest, so a digest pull is served identically forever — and offline once it has been fetched:

    docker pull "$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine@sha256:beefdead…"

    Cross-architecture pulls work too — the cache passes the manifest list through, so --platform selects the variant the same way it would against the upstream:

    docker pull --platform linux/arm64 "$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20"

    Run a throwaway tool straight from the cache — the run itself is ordinary, only the image name is prefixed:

    docker run --rm -it "$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20" sh

    If the container itself installs packages, give it the host’s network and pass the variables through so the tools inside also reach the cache:

    docker run --rm --network=host \ -e PIP_INDEX_URL -e UV_DEFAULT_INDEX -e NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY \ "$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" \ pip download six -d /tmp/wheels
    The first pull is a miss, the rest are hits. A pull the cache has never seen is fetched from the upstream once and stored; every later pull of the same tag or digest — from any machine pointed at the cache — is served from disk, and keeps working after you go offline.
  2. B

    Build an image

    A build has two separate needs, and they fail in different ways. The base image is fetched by the daemon, so it works like a pull — but pass it in as a build argument rather than writing it into the Dockerfile, because the bridge port changes every session. A RUN step is different: it executes in its own network namespace, where 127.0.0.1 is the build container itself and the bridge is simply not there. Without --network=host those steps fail with connection refused.

    # Dockerfile ARG BASE FROM ${BASE} ARG PIP_INDEX_URL RUN pip install --no-cache-dir six
    docker build --network=host \ --build-arg BASE="$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" \ --build-arg PIP_INDEX_URL \ -t myapp:dev .

    The same pattern carries npm (NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY) and Debian or Alpine packages (--build-arg APT_PROXY="$PKGREG_APT_PROXY", then apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$APT_PROXY" update).

    A realistic multi-stage build follows the same rule in each stage that touches the network — the base is a build arg, and any RUN that fetches packages needs --network=host:

    # Dockerfile — build wheels in one stage, copy into a slim runtime ARG BASE FROM ${BASE} AS build ARG PIP_INDEX_URL WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt -w /wheels FROM ${BASE} COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/*.whl

    Two more lines fetch an image, and neither looks like it. A # syntax= parser directive names the frontend BuildKit parses this file with, and it is fetched before the first instruction is read — so a build whose every base came from the cache still goes to Docker Hub for that one, first, and on a host with no route there it fails on line 1. A COPY --from= or a RUN --mount=from= that names an image rather than an earlier stage — COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.10.8 /uv /usr/local/bin/uv — borrows a published image the same way. Both take the prefix a FROM takes; COPY --from=build above names a stage and is not an image at all.

    Neither one can be a build argument, which matters here because the bridge port changes every session. The directive has its own override: BUILDKIT_SYNTAX names the frontend on the command line, so a file that needs one gets it from the cache without an address being written into the file. A borrowed image is refused outright — variable expansion is not supported for --from — so name it in a stage, where a variable does work, and borrow from the stage:

    # Dockerfile — a borrowed image, addressable by build argument ARG BASE ARG UV_IMAGE FROM ${UV_IMAGE} AS uv FROM ${BASE} COPY --from=uv /uv /usr/local/bin/uv
    docker build --network=host \ --build-arg BUILDKIT_SYNTAX="$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/docker/dockerfile:1" \ --build-arg BASE="$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" \ --build-arg UV_IMAGE="$PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY/ghcr/astral-sh/uv:0.10.8" \ -t myapp:dev .

    Both ARGs are declared before the first FROM, which is the only place a variable a FROM reads can live. And BUILDKIT_SYNTAX is worth passing only when the file wants a frontend at all: with no directive and no override, BuildKit uses its built-in one and fetches nothing.

    Every ecosystem at once. Each tool reads its own variable, so one block of ARGs covers all of them and every later RUN is an ordinary command. ARG rather than ENV: a RUN sees the value, and the shipped image does not keep a bridge address that will be dead by the time anyone runs it.

    ARG PKGREG ARG PROJECT=global ARG APT_PROXY ARG PIP_INDEX_URL=${PKGREG}/${PROJECT}/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ ARG UV_DEFAULT_INDEX=${PKGREG}/${PROJECT}/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ ARG NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY=${PKGREG}/${PROJECT}/npm/ ARG GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 ARG GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=url.${PKGREG}/${PROJECT}/git/github.com/.insteadOf ARG GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=https://github.com/ # apt and apk read no index variable, but both honour a proxy — and no_proxy is what # keeps pip and npm going straight to the bridge instead of through it. ARG http_proxy=${APT_PROXY} ARG no_proxy=127.0.0.1,localhost

    Two things are worth knowing about that block. Git has no index variable, but it reads configuration from the environment, so insteadOf can be expressed as GIT_CONFIG_* — which means an unmodified https://github.com/… URL is redirected through the cache, and so are submodules and pip install git+https://…. Alpine ships an https repository list, and an https URL ignores http_proxy, so apk needs one line first:

    RUN sed -i 's/https:/http:/' /etc/apk/repositories \ && apk add --no-cache curl

    In a multi-stage build an ARG is scoped to its stage, so repeat the block in each stage that installs packages.

    Compose builds need the network on the build itself. Pass the values through and set network: host on the build:

    # compose.yaml services: app: build: context: . network: host args: BASE: "${PKGREG_DOCKER_REGISTRY}/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" PIP_INDEX_URL: "${PIP_INDEX_URL}"
    BuildKit changes the network flag, not the idea. With BuildKit (docker buildx build, or DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1) a RUN that needs the bridge uses RUN --network=host … inside the Dockerfile, and the build is invoked with --allow network.host. The base-image build arg is unchanged.
    Build arguments are recorded in the image. Passing an address is fine; never pass a token this way. If the project needs one, build on a host set up as described below, where credentials stay outside the image.
  3. C

    Docker Desktop, remote builders, Compose and CI

    macOS and Windows are always this case. There the daemon runs inside a virtual machine with its own loopback interface, so 127.0.0.1 is not your machine and the bridge simply is not there — a pull fails with dial tcp 127.0.0.1:<port>: connect: connection refused. The same is true of a remote daemon, a docker-container builder and a CI runner. --network=host does not change any of it, so cases A and B do not apply.

    Use the cache’s own address instead. It is stable, so it belongs in a Dockerfile or a Compose file — but Docker has to trust the cache’s CA before it will pull over TLS.

    On a laptop that is one command and no sudo. The client verifies the CA against the fingerprint, then installs it for the Docker daemon alone — one file, nothing else on the machine touched:

    ./pkgreg-client -docker-trust -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT"

    Add -dry-run to see the exact file first, or -uninstall to remove it again. Then restart Docker so the daemon rereads that directory and pull against the cache directly — no bridge, no --network=host, and the address is stable enough to commit:

    docker pull cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20

    The same command works on a Linux Docker host, where the daemon reads /etc/docker/certs.d/ and so it needs sudo. On Windows, Docker Desktop takes registry trust from the Windows certificate store rather than a directory, so use persistent setup there — it imports the CA along with everything else a shared host needs.

    A RUN step here is a different problem from the base image. The base image is Docker’s request, and -docker-trust has already settled it; a RUN is pip or npm making its own TLS connection to the cache, and those tools read their own trust store, not Docker’s. They need the CA.

    Mount it, do not copy it. A COPY writes the certificate into a layer, where it ships with the image to everyone who ever pulls it and outlives every rotation. A BuildKit secret mount exists for exactly this: the file is present for the one RUN that needs it and is in no layer afterwards.

    # syntax=cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/docker/dockerfile:1 # Dockerfile — the CA is mounted for the step, never written into the image. # The directive is line 1 and comes from the cache: BuildKit stops looking for one # after the first comment, and fetches the frontend it names before reading anything. FROM cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ PIP_CERT=/pkgca.crt \ pip install --no-cache-dir \ --index-url https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ six RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ SSL_CERT_FILE=/pkgca.crt \ uv pip install --system \ --default-index https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ six RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ npm install --cafile /pkgca.crt \ --registry https://cache.example.com:8443/global/npm/ left-pad RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ GIT_SSL_CAINFO=/pkgca.crt \ git clone https://cache.example.com:8443/global/git/github.com/pallets/click.git

    The source file is the one -docker-trust already wrote, and it printed the path when it ran:

    # macOS, Docker Desktop docker build --secret id=pkgca,src="$HOME/.docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt" \ -t myapp:dev . # Linux Docker host docker build --secret id=pkgca,src=/etc/docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt \ -t myapp:dev . # inside the pkgreg shell, or on a host with persistent setup, it is already named docker build --secret id=pkgca,src="$PKGREG_CA_FILE" -t myapp:dev .

    apt and apk need none of this. Their proxy is plain HTTP at the cache’s own address, so there is no certificate in the path at all — the same two lines work in any build, on any daemon:

    ARG APT_PROXY RUN apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$APT_PROXY" update \ && apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$APT_PROXY" install -y --no-install-recommends curl # Alpine: same proxy, but switch its repository list to http:// first RUN sed -i 's/https/http/' /etc/apk/repositories \ && http_proxy="$APT_PROXY" apk add --no-cache curl

    A base image that already trusts the cache is the other way to avoid the mount, and is worth building once if your team builds often. On a host with persistent setup the settings are also available as a file to source, so CI jobs need no per-pipeline configuration:

    source /etc/pkgreg/projects/global/env.sh docker compose build

    Because the address is stable, it belongs directly in a Compose file — images pull from the cache, and builds read package indexes from it:

    # compose.yaml — cache address is stable, so it can be committed services: db: image: cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/postgres:16 app: build: context: . # the same mounted CA, declared once for the build secrets: [pkgca] args: BASE: cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine PIP_INDEX_URL: https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ secrets: pkgca: file: /etc/docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt

    CI runners are case C by definition. Trust the CA once in the job (or bake it into the runner image), then pull and build against the cache’s address — no --network=host, no per-pipeline registry config:

    # GitHub Actions step - name: Build through pkgreg run: | sudo ./pkgreg-client -docker-trust -server https://cache.example.com:8443 \ -project global -ca-sha256 "${{ secrets.PKGREG_CA_SHA256 }}" # -docker-trust prints where it wrote the CA; that file is the build secret, # so the runner's image never contains one. docker build \ --secret id=pkgca,src=/etc/docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt \ --build-arg BASE=cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine \ --build-arg PIP_INDEX_URL=https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ \ -t myapp:ci .
    A docker-container buildx builder is also case C. It runs in its own container, so 127.0.0.1 and --network=host do not reach the bridge. Use the cache’s address and hand the CA to the steps that need it with --secret id=pkgca,src="$PKGREG_CA_FILE", exactly as above — a builder that runs elsewhere is no reason to bake a certificate into the image. Pin images by digest in CI so a moved tag never changes a build.
Which case is mine? Docker on this Linux machine and you are in the pkgreg shell → A and B. Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows, a docker-container builder, a remote daemon, or a CI runner → C. When unsure, run case A: if the pull succeeds you are in A, and if it cannot reach the registry you are in C.

shared machines · needs administrator access

Persistent setup, for hosts rather than people.

--persist is the other mode, and it is not part of normal developer setup. Use it when a CI runner, Docker host or shared build machine must keep using pkgreg after every terminal closes. It installs the public CA into the system trust store and Docker’s trust directory, and writes system-wide tool settings — so applying or removing it needs root, and it is the machine’s owner who should do it.

  • the public CA in the OS trust store and in /etc/docker/certs.d/, so Docker and every other tool trust the cache’s real address
  • /etc/pkgreg/projects/<project>/env.sh — the same variables as the temporary shell, but pointing at the cache directly and surviving reboots
  • PKGREG_CA_FILE, for tools that want an explicit CA path rather than the system store
  • optionally a managed hosts entry, with -cache-ip, when site DNS does not resolve the cache name
Show persistent install and uninstall commands

1. Preview without changing anything

Prints every file it would touch. Safe to run unprivileged, and worth reading before the real run.

./pkgreg-client --persist -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -dry-run

2. Apply on Linux or macOS

sudo is required because the CA and the configuration go to protected system locations.

sudo ./pkgreg-client --persist -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" source /etc/pkgreg/projects/global/env.sh

Windows

Preview in a normal PowerShell. To apply, run it without -dry-run in an Administrator PowerShell, then open a new terminal so the machine-wide variables are picked up.

.\pkgreg-client.exe --persist -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -dry-run

3. Remove it

Reverses exactly what was applied, including the CA and the trust refresh. Run the Windows form in an Administrator PowerShell.

sudo ./pkgreg-client --persist -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -uninstall
.\pkgreg-client.exe --persist -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -project global -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -uninstall

The generated setup.sh and setup.ps1 are what these commands run, and both are downloadable from Console → Connect if you want to read or review them before running anything.

troubleshooting

When something does not work.

No download is listed above

Nothing has been published on this instance yet. On the cache host the operator runs pkgreg publish-client; pkgreg doctor confirms it. Do not work around it with insecure package flags — the client is the supported path.

CA fingerprint mismatch

The certificate served does not match the value you passed. Stop and confirm the fingerprint with the operator over a trusted channel. This is the one check that would catch someone impersonating the cache, so do not bypass it.

server must use https

The -server value must be the cache’s origin with its scheme and port and nothing else — no path, no trailing slash, no credentials. The command in step 2 is already in that form.

401 on every package request

The project requires an access token. Create a read token in Connect and pass it with -token-file, as described in step 2.

connection refused inside docker build

A RUN step cannot see your loopback interface. Add --network=host to the build, or, if the daemon is not on this machine, use case C under Docker.

connection refused on docker pull

If the address is 127.0.0.1 and you are on macOS or Windows, this is expected rather than broken: the daemon runs in a virtual machine whose loopback is not yours. Run pkgreg-client -docker-trust and pull from the cache’s own address instead — case C under Docker. On macOS that needs no sudo and changes nothing outside Docker.

A tool ignores the cache and goes upstream

Something is overriding the session — a pip.conf, .npmrc, or uv.toml in your project or home directory, or a corporate HTTP_PROXY. The client keeps 127.0.0.1 and localhost in NO_PROXY, but a file that pins an index URL wins over the environment. Compare env | grep ^PIP_ against what the tool reports it is using.

How do I undo the normal setup?

Type exit. There is nothing to uninstall, and any second shell you opened from another terminal was never affected. Only --persist changes a machine, and only --persist -uninstall reverses it.

Download. Start. Exit.

That is the whole developer setup. Docker and shared hosts are the two exceptions, and both are above.
